cim: Algorithmic Constitutionalism: Reimagining Constitutional Authority in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
cim_eredeti: Algorithmic Constitutionalism: Reimagining Constitutional Authority in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
—Forhad Hossain, Lecturer, University of Asia Pacific, Bangladesh

Public authorities increasingly use automation software in governance. Welfare agencies use Artificial Intelligence (AI) to flag risky claimants, tax authorities use it to select returns for audit, and courts read risk scores when sentencing. These tools promise efficiency. However, recent scholarship warns that using AI in the name of efficiency may turn the rule of law into rule by law (Smuha). Her analysis raises a question that existing constitutional theory does not fully answer. Existing conceptions of constitutionalism are framed to limit identifiable rulers acting through recognizable institutions. What happens to those limits when power is exercised through a model that officials cannot fully explain, built by a private company that no voter chose?

In this post, I use the term algorithmic constitutionalism to offer a framework that subjects public power exercised by algorithmic systems to constitutional limits. The framework is based on the existing vocabulary of constitutionalism that limits public power: requirements of legality, accountability, justification, and rights protection. The term is not new. It has been used by Perez and Wimer for a design approach that builds constitutional safeguards into the code of AI models used by private platforms. My use is different. I do not intend to constitutionalize algorithms. Instead, this post offers a framework for constitutionalizing the State’s use of algorithmic power so that AI systems are answerable to the Constitution.

Limiting power is constitutionalism’s core purpose. Locke tied the legitimate exercise of power to standing and published laws. In Federalist No. 51, Madison argued that institutions should check one another, so that “ambition must be made to counteract ambition”. Dicey placed ordinary law at the center of the rule of law to limit public authority. Each account assumes that power has an author: someone makes the decision, and someone can be held answerable.

Over the years, constitutionalism has adapted to shifting power dynamics. The literature on constitutional change warns against taking labels at face value, since what is presented as an amendment may, in substance, dismember the constitution (R. Albert). The same lesson runs in reverse for algorithmic governance. With AI, power can be exercised through algorithms without any textual amendment or anything labeled a constitutional change. The text remains the same, but real power moves beyond it. As Ginsburg and Huq show, constitutional design can hinder or hasten a democracy’s decline. In the same way, the algorithmic systems reshaping that design evoke a constitutional question as much as a technical one. Furthermore, Landau’s account of abusive constitutionalism, extended with Dixon in Abusive Constitutional Borrowing, explains how democracy can be eroded stealthily behind liberal-democratic forms. Algorithmic systems can do the same, wrapping discretionary power in the language of neutrality and efficiency. Thus, constitutional law must watch them as closely as it watches amendments.

The framework proposed in this post engages with three bodies of literature. First, it is narrower than Giovanni De Gregorio’s account of digital constitutionalism, which addresses the constitutional response to private platform power (such as Meta). My concern is the state’s own use of algorithms in its governance. Second, it draws on Danielle Citron’s technological due process, which showed that automated systems merge adjudication and rulemaking and escape the procedural protections of both. Third, its closest antecedent is Aziz Huq’s evaluation of the US rights doctrines, including privacy, equality, and due process, established for human decision-making, and their compatibility with the machine-learning state. I add a comparative lens: algorithmic systems as a channel of informal constitutional change and abusive constitutionalism, and the structural question of how the separation of powers and judicial review must adapt.

Governments now use algorithmic systems to assess welfare eligibility, screen visa applications, detect fraud, direct police patrols, and inform sentencing. Beyond assisting officials, these systems categorize people based on data and allocate resources, functions traditionally performed by public authorities.

For instance, the Dutch SyRI system linked data held by different public authorities to produce risk reports on possible social security fraud and other offences under tax and labor law. In 2020, the District Court of The Hague found that the SyRI legislation breached Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights because it failed to strike a fair balance between protecting private life and preventing fraud. Similarly, from 2015, Australia’s Robodebt scheme used automated income averaging to raise welfare debts, until the Federal Court found it unlawful in 2019. The Royal Commission described it as “a crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal.”

The established conception of administrative law is that every decision has an author who provides reasons, and that the decision can be challenged. Algorithmic systems strain this conception. A claimant refused by an official can ask why. But when the refusal comes from a risk score generated by a model trained on data the agency may not even hold, the question “why?” becomes a constitutional one: who exercised this power, and who answers for it?

More than twenty-five years ago, Lawrence Lessig argued that code regulates our conduct alongside law. Later, Jack Balkin described an “Algorithmic Society” in which public and private organizations govern people through technology, with deep asymmetries of computational power and information between those who govern and those being governed. His point matters here: we need laws that govern the organizations and authorities that use algorithms, not the algorithms themselves. This mirrors the premise of algorithmic constitutionalism.

Smuha distinguishes between rule of law and rule by law. She argues that the former limits power, ensures equal application, and provides legal certainty, whereas the latter keeps law as an instrument but strips it of its protective purpose. Algorithmic rule by law can arise in two ways. It can be negligent, when a well-meaning government scales up a rigid policy, or deliberate, when an illiberal government uses technical opacity to adopt measures it could not defend openly. Both paths concern constitutional theory because they shift discretionary power from civil servants to coders.

When a government says that “the system flagged it” as a defense to a decision, it offers a procedural explanation, not a justification. Constitutional law asks a prior question: was the system lawfully authorized? For example, a discriminatory immigration decision may pass through officials, software developers, data providers, machine-learning models, and contractors. Each can blame another. This creates power without a responsible author, which constitutionalism is meant to prevent.

Opacity compounds the problem. In State v. Loomis (2016), the Wisconsin Supreme Court allowed a sentencing court to use the COMPAS risk score with only a written warning about the tool’s limitations. Because of its trade secret status, neither the court nor the defendant knew the tool’s methodology or how it generated the score. As a result, the justification for public decisions gives way to deference to a product.

Robert Post’s distinction between the constitutional domain of democracy and the managerial domain helps explain what is at stake. In the managerial domain, law is measured by whether it achieves set goals. Algorithmic governance pulls welfare entitlement and criminal punishment into that domain, treating them as tools to achieve set goals. The domain of democracy, by contrast, requires justifying decisions to those affected.
